newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Commodities seen driven by stocks in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Commodities seen driven by stocks in 1997.

text.p: The outlook for world commodity prices going into 1997 is for steady-to-higher prices, with low inventories in the agriculture and energy sectors, and high demand from developing countries, still the driving factors, analysts said.
These factors have resulted in returns on investments in commodities as an asset class running well above returns on US equities or bonds in 1996, analysts said.

"Since the end of June 1995, commodity returns have outpaced the returns of virtually all major equity markets and most bond markets, except for a few emerging markets," Goldman Sachs commodity research director Steve Strongin said.
"More important, the factors driving strong commodity performance are still in place as we enter 1997."

Buying and rolling nearby CME Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) futures each month, as a proxy for investing in commodities, has produced a 44.72 percent return year-to-date in 1996, well above the 19.61 percent return on S&P500 index equities or the 4.40 percent return on bonds.
The GSCI, representing a basket of 22 commodities with a 49 percent weighting in the energy sector, was trading around 223.73 early Wednesday, after seeing a new record high at 229.71 last week.

The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index (CRB), a basket of 17 commodities with a heavier weighting in agricultural products, was at 244.84 points early Wednesday, up from 12 month lows seen at 235.99 in mid-November, but well off the eight year highs at 263.79 seen in April this year.
"Commodity prices probably remain in their long term stair-step uptrend, with the energy sector the leader right now," Merill Lynch commodities strategist Bill O'Neill said.
"But the low growth/low inflation outlook for developed countries will probably mean no great explosion in demand."

Inventories in the energy and agriculture sectors remain near historic lows and global demand remains high, pushing many commodities into a backwardated price structure, where the price for immediate delivery is higher than the price for deferred delivery.

"In short, (in the energy sector) the story today is to be found in the spreads (between nearby and forward prices) and inventories," said Philip Verleger of oil industry consultants, Charles River Associates in Washington DC.

The market has over-emphasized the relatively weak G-7 economic growth and the low level of G-7 inflation, rather than appreciating the impact on inventories of strong global demand arising from emerging markets, analysts said.
As a result, "investor returns have exceeded, and are expected to continue to substantially exceed, changes in underlying spot prices," Strongin said.

"The overall pattern of returns in 1997 will likely mimic that of 1996, where spot prices are up only 6.5 percent year-to-date, while investor returns are 32.5 percent as spot shortages rather than secular price trends have dominated returns," he said.
ENERGY SECTOR
For example, crude oil prices saw five year highs this despite the partial return of Iraqi oil to world markets, analysts noted.
Nearby NYMEX crude oil futures saw a five year high at $26.10 a barrel on October 22, while nearby IPE Brent futures saw a post-Gulf War high at $25.06 a barrel on October 15.
The average price of benchmark WTI (West Texas Intermediate) crude oil so far in 1996 is $21.81 a barrel, up $3.40 on 1995.

But the average backwardation (spot WTI less 12 month WTI price) has been $3.38 a barrel, against an average backwardation in 1995 of only 83 cents a barrel, and an average backwardation since 1989, excluding the Gulf War, of only 78 cents a barrel, Verleger said.
"Hence a full 80 percent of the spot price increase can be ascribed to the reduction in inventories," he said.
A return to more normal stock levels in 1997 may cause WTI oil prices to drop back toward the nine year mean of $19.31 a barrel, Verleger said.

"The likelihood of such a price decline is increased by Iraq's return to the market, a political and economic cycle leading to slightly lower economic growth, and the rise in non-OPEC production," he said.
AGRICULTURAL SECTOR

In the agricultural sector, low stocks and high demand led to nearby CBOT wheat prices seeing a record high at 750 cents a bushel, while nearby CBOT corn prices rose to a multi-year high at 555 cents a bushel.
The higher grain prices generated higher plantings this year which will modestly undermine the potential for shortages next year, analysts said.
"But despite the markets focus on potential Southern-hemisphere (grain) supplies, demand is again growing rapidly and production sources are limited," Strongin said.
METALS SECTOR
The metals sector is seen remaining weak though, as industrial demand in Europe and Japan is slow, analysts said.
"The 1980s growth cycle was led by Europe and Japan and hence was very metals intensive," Strongin said.

"The current cycle is energy and agriculture intensive, and as a result there is a deficit of past investment in the agriculture and energy sectors, leading to potentially significantly higher prices as the necessary incentive to spur investment," he said.
-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 1-212-859-1641;
